newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds and dollar fall; oil jumps.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds and dollar fall; oil jumps.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average topped 6,000 points Monday for the first time before ending lower on profit-taking, but the Nasdaq index scored its first record close in four months as technology stocks rallied.
Bond prices and the dollar fell. Oil prices soared on worries that a storm would disrupt tanker deliveries in the Gulf of Mexico.

The 30-share Dow index fell 13.05 points to close at 5,979.81 after a brief run up to 6,002.17. The Nasdaq Composite index, laden with high-tech company stocks, rose 3.31 to 1,250.87, beating its June 5 record of 1,249.15.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,208 to 1,123 on moderate volume of 380 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said the Dow was due for a pause after setting its 27th record close for the year Friday at 5,992.86 as a weaker-than-expected report on September jobs lessened Wall Street's fears that the Federal Reserve would need to raise interest rates to slow the economy's growth.

"We're recovering from a little nosebleed after Friday's highs and some people are taking profits off the table," said Ken Ducey, head of trading at BT Brokerage. "People seem fairly convinced sometime this week we'll close above 6,000."

Other stock market gauges also set new milestones, with the Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks gaining 1.91 points to 703.37, its fifth record close in the past six trading sessions. The NYSE Composite index was at a new high, up 0.58 to 374.74.
The Dow's rise through the 6,000 level came just days before the market marks the sixth anniversary this Friday of its current bull run.
The moonshot-like jump in the Dow started on Oct. 11, 1990, with the index climbing from 2,365 and the S&P 500 index from 295.
William LeFevre, senior analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum was unfazed by the 6,000 milestone and upcoming anniversary.
"It's a bull market. Relax and enjoy it," he said.
The bond market also yielded to profit-taking. The bellwether 30-year Treasury lost nearly half a point, raising its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.75 percent on Friday.
In currency markets, the dollar fell against the Japanese yen after two senior Japanese politicians suggested interest rates in Japan might soon head higher.
Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japan, declined to comment on the rate talk.

The dollar slid as low as 111.05 yen in New York but later trimmed its losses. In late New York trading, the dollar fetched 111.19 yen and 1.5312 German marks, down from 111.79 yen and 1.5323 marks late Friday.
Higher Japanese rates would make some investments in Japan more attractive, boosting demand for yen.
Oil prices jumped on worries about a tropical storm threatening to disrupt tanker deliveries in the Gulf of Mexico.
"Basically, the sky's the limit," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst at ING Derivatives in New York. "It's low stocks, cold weather, and it's technical strength."

Tropical Storm Josephine, with 70 mph winds, was centred 175 miles south southwest of Apalachicola, Fla., late Monday and was likely to reach hurricane strength by the evening, weather forecasters said.
November crude oil at NYMEX closed 51 cents higher at $25.24 a barrel after rising to a contract high of $25.28.
